blocks.text: A fuel attendant's meter is set 2% high. Every single customer is overcharged by exactly 2%, and no amount of double-checking one purchase will reveal it. That is a systematic error, and it behaves completely differently from the ordinary scatter you get when you read a scale by eye.

blocks.markdown:
No measurement is exact. **Error** in physics does not mean a mistake — it means the unavoidable difference between a measured value and the true value. Your job is not to eliminate error (impossible) but to know how big it is and to report it honestly.

There are two families of error, and they need different treatment.

blocks.title: Systematic and random error
blocks.text: A systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by roughly the same amount — a zero error, a badly calibrated meter, a stopwatch that runs slow. Repeating readings will never remove it. A random error scatters readings above and below the true value — reaction time, parallax, fluctuating conditions. Taking the mean of many readings reduces it.

Reaction time, judging a scale, draughts

blocks.caption: Comparing the two types of error

blocks.markdown:
### Accuracy is not precision

**Accuracy** is how close a reading is to the true value. **Precision** is how closely repeated readings agree with one another.

A micrometer with a 0.5 mm zero error is very *precise* — every reading agrees to 0.01 mm — but badly *inaccurate*, because every reading is 0.5 mm too big. A worn metre rule read carefully may be accurate on average but imprecise. You need both.

Percentage error when a true or accepted value is given

blocks.title: Percentage error in a micrometer measurement
blocks.prompt: A wire's diameter is measured as 0.50 mm using a micrometer screw gauge of least count 0.01 mm. Calculate the percentage error in the measurement.

steps.text: Write the formula for percentage error using the instrument uncertainty.
The uncertainty is the least count of the instrument, 0.01 mm, and the measured value is 0.50 mm.
Interpret: a 2% error is acceptable, but measuring a wire ten times thinner with the same instrument would give a 20% error — which is why very thin objects are stacked before measuring.

blocks.markdown:
### Combining errors

When quantities are multiplied or divided, **add the percentage errors**. So for the area of a rectangle,

$$\frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{\Delta l}{l} + \frac{\Delta w}{w}$$

This tells you which measurement to improve. If one term dominates the total, spending effort on the other is wasted.

### Significant figures

Your answer can be no more precise than your least precise data. If a question gives you $2.5\ \text{m}$ and $4.0\ \text{s}$ (both two significant figures), do not report $0.625\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$ — report $0.63\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$.

Zeros between digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point count; leading zeros never do. So $0.004530$ has **four** significant figures: 4, 5, 3 and the final 0.

blocks.title: WAEC practical tip
blocks.text: Carry extra digits through a calculation and round only at the very end. Rounding at each step accumulates rounding error and can shift your final answer out of the accepted range. In the practical paper, quote the same number of decimal places as your instrument allows in every row of your table — an inconsistent table loses marks even when the numbers are right.

points: Systematic errors shift every reading the same way and are not removed by repeating; random errors scatter readings and are reduced by averaging.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is agreement between repeated readings. An instrument can be precise yet inaccurate.
Percentage error = uncertainty ÷ measured value × 100, or |measured − true| ÷ true × 100 when a true value is quoted.
For products and quotients, add the percentage errors of the individual quantities.
Report answers to the number of significant figures justified by the least precise data, and round only at the end.
